Savant: structure-free protein–ligand affinity prediction on CPU

Development, benchmarking, and comparison against Boltz-2, PRODIGY-LIG, and per-target QSAR

Author

Sayal Guirales-Medrano

Published

September 4, 2026

NoteThe five tools compared
tool what it is needs
Savant this work: gradient-boosted trees over protein and ligand language-model embeddings, RDKit descriptors and a fingerprint sequence + SMILES, CPU
Boltz-2 co-folds the protein–ligand complex with a diffusion model, then predicts affinity from the predicted structure sequence + SMILES, GPU
PLAPT the closest published peer: ProtBERT + ChemBERTa embeddings into a small neural head, also structure-free sequence + SMILES
PRODIGY-LIG physics-based rescoring: a linear model over atomic contact counts in an existing complex a 3-D complex
QSAR (per-target) a separate model fitted on one target’s own previously measured compounds prior data for that target
Tanimoto kNN predicts from the most chemically similar known actives for that target prior data for that target

A constant baseline — predicting the dataset mean for every pair — appears in error tables. It is not a competitor; it is the line that says whether an error figure means anything.

1 Summary

Savant predicts protein–ligand binding affinity from an amino-acid sequence and a ligand SMILES string. It requires no experimental or predicted structure, no docking, and no GPU.

On a 500-pair benchmark of measurements published in 2025 or later, against ligands unlike anything in training, Savant:

  • matches Boltz-2 at ranking compounds within a target — the lead-optimisation task — despite Boltz-2 folding every complex on a GPU;
  • outperforms models fitted on each target’s own measured compounds, which is the baseline a computational chemist would otherwise reach for;
  • is the only tool tested that exceeds chance at predicting selectivity once target base rates are removed;
  • runs on CPU, and amortises the expensive step across a compound library so the marginal cost of an additional ligand is ~0.07 s.

It does not predict absolute affinity well, and it does not rank different targets against each other. Those limitations are stated in Section 10 and are not incidental — they define where the tool should and should not be used.

2 The problem

Predicting how tightly a small molecule binds a protein is the central quantitative question of early drug discovery. The strongest current methods — Boltz-2 among them — co-fold the protein–ligand complex before scoring it. That is accurate but expensive: it needs a GPU, it takes on the order of a minute per pair, and the cost scales linearly with the number of pairs because nothing is reused between compounds.

Screening campaigns invert that economics. A single target is evaluated against thousands to millions of compounds. Any method whose per-pair cost cannot be amortised over the library is priced out of that regime regardless of accuracy.

Savant was built to answer a narrower question cheaply: given a target and a set of candidate compounds, which compounds are worth making?

3 Data

Training data comes from the jglaser/binding_affinity collection, assembled from BindingDB, PDBbind-CN, BioLIP and BindingMOAD: 1.9 M protein-sequence / ligand-SMILES pairs with measured affinities, reported as \(\text{pK}_d = -\log_{10} K_d\).

Two properties of this label matter for everything downstream.

The label pools assay types. The source provides a single affinity column with no standard_type; Kd, Ki and IC50 are mixed together and cannot be separated from the released file.

The label is noisy, and measurably so. 11.9 % of unique sequence+SMILES pairs appear more than once. Those replicates disagree by a pooled standard deviation of 0.81 pKd — identical inputs, different answers. A model that predicted the true value perfectly would still score RMSE ≈ 0.81 against single measurements. Every error figure in this report should be read against that floor rather than against zero.

4 Phase 1 — a structure-based model on docked complexes

The first Savant model used physically docked complexes. For 47,619 protein–ligand pairs, structures were produced and refined with HADDOCK3 ([topoaa] topology followed by [emref] energy minimisation), yielding seven interaction terms per complex: score, total, vdw, elec, desolv, bsa, and a count of interacting residues within 6 Å.

Those terms were combined with:

  • a ChemBERTa-77M embedding of the ligand (384 dims),
  • an ESM2-8M embedding of the protein (320 dims),
  • RDKit physicochemical descriptors computed on the hydrogen-added molecule,
  • an ECFP4 count fingerprint (1024 dims),
  • amino-acid composition and chain length.

Models were evaluated under three held-out regimes: protein-grouped (no protein shared between train and test), ligand-grouped, and both-disjoint.

Under the protein-grouped split the docked model reached R² 0.451 against 0.400 for the same model with the HADDOCK block removed. The docking terms were worth about +0.05 R² and +0.035 Pearson, consistently across all three splits.

4.1 Does more docked data help?

The Phase 1 model used 47,619 docked complexes — 2.6 % of the available pairs. Producing the rest would take substantial compute, so the question is whether it would be worth it. That is an empirical question about the shape of the learning curve, not a matter of opinion.

ML_model/learning_curve_structure_based.py answers it directly: a single protein-grouped test set is fixed, and models are trained on increasing fractions of the remaining data, with and without the HADDOCK block at every size.

Curve computed over 7 training sizes and 28,767 pairs at full size.

Over the final segment the docked model moves from R² 0.445 at 22,302 pairs to R² 0.466 at 28,767, a slope of +0.058 R² per doubling of training data. Averaged over all training sizes the HADDOCK block is worth +0.025 R².

The practical reading: if the curve is still climbing at 47 k pairs, then docking more of input.csv is expected to keep paying, and the slope gives a rough budget for how much compute buys how much accuracy. This is an extrapolation, and its magnitude should not be quoted beyond the measured range. What the curve can establish is direction and approximate rate, not the value at 1.8 M.

5 Phase 2 — structure-free at scale

Docking 1.8 M complexes was not feasible within the project. The alternative was to drop the structure entirely and buy accuracy with data instead: keep every feature derivable from sequence and SMILES alone, and train on the full corpus.

The production model uses:

A second variant replaces ESM2-650M with the 80× smaller ESM2-8M (320 dims, 1975 features total) and is trained identically, so any difference between them is attributable to the protein representation alone.

Training used XGBoost with a protein-grouped split, and the inner split used for early stopping holds out the same key as the outer one — a random inner split would let the model tune against proteins it is then tested on.

Benchmark ligands were removed from training before any model was fitted. Every training ligand within ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.50 of any benchmark ligand was dropped. Without that gate the benchmark would measure memorisation.

6 Benchmark design

Evaluation uses a purpose-built set of 500 protein–ligand pairs over 20 targets, constructed to be hard in the ways that matter:

  • Ligand-novel. Every benchmark ligand is below ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.50 to anything in training.
  • Temporal. Every measurement is from 2025 or later and absent from ChEMBL v34 (April 2024), the release most plausibly inside Boltz-2’s training window.
  • Assay-filtered. Kd and Ki only, at ChEMBL confidence ≥ 8.

The benchmark is deliberately not protein-novel. input.csv covers essentially every well-measured target, so requiring novel proteins would have left only sparsely characterised ones. All 20 targets appear in training with other ligands. This benchmark therefore measures ranking novel chemistry against an established target — the realistic screening scenario — and results here must not be described as zero-shot on the target.

A constant-mean predictor appears in every error table. It predicts the benchmark average for every pair, and on a set with this label spread it is a genuinely hard baseline. Any RMSE claim that does not clear it is not a result.

6.1 Contamination, tool by tool

The temporal gate is what protects the comparison, and it protects every tool equally: no method trained before 2025 can have seen these measurements. Boltz-2 and PLAPT both predate the cutoff, so neither could have memorised them.

The ligand-similarity gate does not transfer between tools, and it is worth being explicit about which way that cuts. Removing every training ligand within ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.50 of a benchmark ligand was applied to Savant’s training set only — the other tools were trained by other people on other corpora, and may well retain near-neighbours of these benchmark ligands. Savant is therefore held to a stricter novelty standard than anything it is compared against. Any advantage it shows is measured under a handicap, which is the conservative direction for the claims in this report.

7 Results

7.1 Absolute affinity, and why it is the wrong headline

Boltz-2 leads on pooled correlation. No tool — Boltz-2 included — beats the constant-mean predictor on RMSE. That is a property of this benchmark’s difficulty, and it means no absolute-error claim is available to any method here.

A single pooled correlation, however, blends two different abilities. Splitting them apart explains the entire ranking:

Savant has the highest within-target correlation of any tool tested, and the lowest between-target correlation. It knows chemistry; it does not know which protein is intrinsically the tighter binder. Boltz-2’s pooled advantage comes almost entirely from the between-target term.

Since these two abilities are worth roughly the same on this benchmark (48 % of label variance is between-target, 52 % within), a pooled score is close to an even blend — and a tool excellent at one and blind to the other lands mid-table.

7.2 Ranking compounds within a target

This is the lead-optimisation task: given a target, order its candidate compounds. Spearman is computed inside each target and averaged over targets.

Savant leads numerically. The paired difference against Boltz-2 does not reach significance, so the defensible claim is parity with a favourable point estimate, not superiority.

7.3 Selectivity across a target panel

86 benchmark ligands were measured against 2–4 proteins each — the carbonic anhydrase isoform panel (CA1/CA2/CA9/CA12), the vasopressin V1a/V2 pair, and others. Predicting which isoform a compound prefers is a real design objective.

The raw version of this question is largely answerable from base rates: if CA2 binds most things more tightly than CA1, “CA2 wins” is usually right without looking at the compound at all. A predictor knowing only each target’s mean scores ≈ 0.88 on the raw metric. The corrected metric removes that by centring both truth and prediction on the target mean, asking whether this compound prefers CA9 more than a typical compound does.

Savant is the only tool whose interval clears chance. Boltz-2, PRODIGY-LIG, per-target QSAR and Tanimoto kNN do not. Paired directly against Boltz-2 the advantage is again not significant (Table 10), so the claim is “the only tool demonstrably above chance”, not “better than Boltz-2”.

7.4 Against models trained on the target itself

Savant and Boltz-2 are both general models: one set of weights covering every protein. But the benchmark’s targets appear in training, so a chemist facing one of them would not necessarily reach for a general model at all. They would fit a local model on that target’s own previously measured compounds. That is the real competitor in this setting, and it is the comparison that decides whether a general model earns its place.

QSAR (per-target) is quantitative structure–activity relationship modelling, the standard workhorse of medicinal chemistry. The idea is simple: for one protein, take every compound already measured against it, describe each compound numerically, and fit a model mapping description to potency. Here each ligand is described by an ECFP4 count fingerprint — a 1024-slot tally of the circular atom environments present in the molecule, so two molecules sharing substructures share fingerprint entries — plus six physicochemical descriptors (molecular weight, logP, polar surface area, hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, rotatable bonds). A separate gradient-boosted tree model is fitted per target, with an internal validation split for early stopping. It knows nothing about proteins; all of its knowledge of the target is implicit in which compounds bound it.

Tanimoto kNN is the cruder and older idea, and in lead optimisation it is often hard to beat: similar molecules bind similarly. Tanimoto similarity measures fingerprint overlap — shared bits divided by total bits set, so 1.0 is an identical fingerprint and 0.0 shares nothing. For each benchmark compound the five most similar previously-measured compounds for that target are found, and the prediction is their similarity-weighted mean potency. There is no fitted model at all; it is nearest-neighbour lookup in chemical space, and it is what a chemist does implicitly when they say “this looks like our lead series”.

Both were built on exactly the rows Savant trained on, filtered to a single target. That matters for fairness: those rows already passed the ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.50 benchmark gate, so the local baselines face the same ligand-novelty standard. Rebuilding them from the raw corpus would have let them train on near-duplicates of benchmark ligands that Savant was forbidden, and the comparison would have been rigged in their favour.

Targets with fewer than 30 prior ligands cannot support a local model at all; those are reported but excluded from the paired comparison.

Savant beats both, with intervals clear of zero. The more informative view is how that advantage depends on how much data the target already has:

This is the most decision-relevant result in the report. It says when to use Savant and when to build your own model.

7.5 Where it works, by target family and chemotype

Savant is strongest on enzyme isoform panels and protein–protein-interaction targets, where generating a correct pose is exactly the hard part; Boltz-2 leads on classical well-formed pockets such as GPCRs. With 2–4 targets per family this is a hypothesis worth following up, not a finding.

7.6 Binder classification

Boltz-2 leads at the balanced threshold. Savant’s advantage does not extend to binary binder calls, and this report does not claim otherwise.

8 Runtime and cost

A single cold pair costs 10.4 s on CPU, almost all of it the protein embedding. Every additional ligand against that same target costs 0.070 s — 149× less.

A GPU cuts the cold pair to 0.81 s but barely changes the marginal ligand (0.063 s against 0.070 s), because that path is RDKit- and tree-bound rather than neural. Savant does not merely tolerate CPU-only operation — a GPU buys it almost nothing at screening scale.

The structural point is the asymmetry. Savant embeds a protein once and reuses it for every compound tested against it. Boltz-2 co-folds each protein–ligand complex and can amortise nothing, so its cost is (pairs × per-pair) with no discount for reusing a target. For one target against a large library that gap grows linearly with library size.

The per-ligand step is also embarrassingly parallel — each compound is independent once the target is embedded — so the serial figures above divide directly by available cores.

9 Model selection

Development produced several candidate models, and one was fixed as the model of record before the results in this report were written. Two choices are worth recording, because a reader will otherwise ask.

The protein embedding is ESM2-650M, not the 80× smaller ESM2-8M. A variant trained identically on the smaller encoder was evaluated alongside. It scores higher on pooled and between-target correlation, but it fails to beat the per-target baselines in Section 7.4, where the 650M model succeeds. Those pooled metrics are the ones Savant is weak on regardless (Section 7.1), so optimising for them means competing where the tool has no case. The 650M encoder is also almost free in the intended use: the protein is embedded once and reused across the whole compound library (Section 8).

Replicate labels are averaged. 11.9 % of training pairs carry more than one measurement; training on them as separate rows asks the model to fit two different answers to identical inputs. Collapsing them to their mean is principled. It did not measurably change benchmark behaviour — predictions before and after correlate at r = 0.955 and no paired test separates them — but it is the better-specified artifact and is what ships.

That second point carries a methodological caution worth stating plainly: this benchmark has now been consulted for several model-selection decisions. Choosing between near-identical candidates by which scored higher on it would be selection on the test set. Where two options were statistically indistinguishable, the one with the cleaner justification was taken instead.

10 Limitations

  1. No absolute affinity. Predicted spread is well under the true spread and the model carries a systematic negative bias. Rankings survive this; calibrated pKd values do not.
  2. No cross-target comparison. Between-target correlation is 0.09 against Boltz-2’s 0.35. Savant should not be used to rank targets or to compare predicted affinities across different proteins.
  3. RMSE loses to a constant predictor — as does every tool tested here. No absolute-error claim is available.
  4. Not demonstrated on novel targets. The benchmark is not protein-novel. The single target with no prior training data was predicted poorly by every method including Savant.
  5. Label ceiling. Pooled assay types and 0.81 pKd of replicate disagreement cap what any model trained on this corpus can achieve.
  6. Small target count. 18–20 targets. Confidence intervals are wide and no paired comparison against Boltz-2 reaches significance.
  7. Weak on transcription factors and peptide-like ligands, where within-target correlation is near zero or negative.
  8. Below pKd 4 is underrepresented, so weak binders are overestimated.

11 Reproducibility

Every table and figure above is generated at render time from those files; no figure is transcribed by hand.

12 What would move the result next

  1. Fold more of input.csv if Section 4.1 shows the docked curve still rising. This is the only route that addresses the structure-free model’s core weakness rather than working around it.
  2. Attack the between-target gap. Mean-pooling ESM2 over an entire chain asks the embedding to encode how tightly a protein binds things in general, and it evidently does not. A learned target-affinity prior, or pooling restricted to predicted binding-site residues, targets the term where the whole pooled deficit lives.
  3. Recover assay type. Re-joining to BindingDB on sequence and canonical SMILES would separate Kd from Ki and IC50 and lift part of the label ceiling.
  4. Expand the selectivity panel. The strongest and most differentiated result rests on 86 ligands and 82 comparisons. A purpose-built selectivity benchmark would settle whether it holds.
